name: Loop-Until-Done
description: A worker drafts, an independent judge decides whether the exit bar is met, and the engine repeats the pair until the judge approves or the pass budget runs out.

charter.mission: Converge on work that meets a stated bar by iterating a draft/judge pair, with the bar written down before the first draft and applied by someone who did not do the drafting. The loop stops when the judge approves, not when the worker feels finished.
conventions: The judge decides; the worker revises. A judge that edits the draft has stopped being an independent check, and a worker that overrules the judge has removed the loop's only exit condition.
Every rejection names blocking items concretely enough that the next draft can act on them. "Not good enough" is not a blocking item.
Each pass carries what the last one learned in its `handoff` field. A pass that repeats a rejected approach has spent budget for nothing.
nonGoals: Widening the exit bar mid-loop to make a draft pass — the bar is set in the brief and only an operator amendment changes it.
Perfecting the work beyond the bar: the judge approves the first draft that clears it, not the best draft imaginable.

invariants.statement: The judge context never edits the work it reviews. It reads the draft's output and the exit bar, and returns a verdict with blocking items.
Every pass ends with the judge's captured verdict. The engine reads that verdict to decide whether the loop continues; a pass that ends without one cannot be settled.

sourcesOfTruth.label: Loop brief
sourcesOfTruth.description: The objective the worker drafts against and the exit bar the judge applies: what has to be true for the work to be done, stated so a third party can check it.

sourcesOfTruth.label: Repository engineering contract
sourcesOfTruth.description: The engineering contract every draft has to satisfy — typing, testing, and architecture boundaries.

executionContexts.title: State the objective and the exit bar
executionContexts.description: Read the loop brief and restate, in checkable terms, what the work has to achieve and what the judge will hold it to.
executionContexts.acceptanceCriteria: The objective is stated in one sentence that names the outcome rather than the activity, and the exit bar is stated so that a reviewer who did not do the work can decide whether it is met without asking a follow-up question. Both are captured as structured output.

outputSchema.description: The contract every pass of the loop works against.

objective.description: What the work has to achieve, in one sentence.

exitBar.description: The condition the judge applies to decide whether a draft is done.

executionContexts.title: Draft or revise the work
executionContexts.description: Produce the next revision: the first draft on pass 1, and on every later pass a revision that addresses the judge's blocking items.
executionContexts.acceptanceCriteria: The revision addresses every blocking item the previous pass's judge recorded, or says explicitly why an item is not actionable. The work itself is complete enough to be judged — not a plan for work. The captured output summarizes what changed this pass and hands the next pass what it needs to know.

outputSchema.description: What this pass produced, for the judge and for the next pass.

passSummary.description: What this revision changed, in the objective's terms.

handoff.description: What the next pass should know: what was tried, what was ruled out, and why.

executionContexts.title: Judge the revision against the exit bar
executionContexts.description: Independently decide whether this revision meets the exit bar, and either approve or name what blocks approval.
executionContexts.acceptanceCriteria: The verdict is decided against the exit bar stated in the brief, not against the reviewer's own preferences, and it is reached by inspecting the work rather than by reading the worker's summary of it. A `revise` verdict names at least one blocking item, each concrete enough to act on; an `approved` verdict names none.

outputSchema.description: The judge's verdict. The engine reads `verdict` to decide whether the loop continues.

verdict.description: `approved` ends the loop; `revise` sends the blocking items back to the worker.

blocking.description: What blocks approval, one item per problem. Empty when approved.

handoff.description: Context for the next pass beyond the blocking list — what the judge looked at, and what would change its mind.

executionContexts.title: Publish the approved result
executionContexts.description: Take the approved revision as final and record the outcome for whoever comes next.
executionContexts.acceptanceCriteria: The summary describes what was delivered and cites the approving verdict rather than restating the drafting history. Nothing is re-litigated: the judge's approval is the decision, and this context does not reopen it.

delivered.description: What was delivered, in the objective's terms.

tasks.title: State the objective and the exit bar
tasks.instructions:
Read the loop brief named as rank 1 in the charter.

Restate the objective in one sentence that names the OUTCOME, not the activity: "the projection warms in under 200ms" rather than "improve the projection". Then state the exit bar — the condition the judge will apply to every revision. A bar that cannot be checked without asking you a follow-up question is not a bar; rewrite it until a reviewer who has not seen this conversation could apply it.

If the brief leaves the bar genuinely ambiguous, choose the stricter reading and say so in the summary rather than leaving the loop to discover the ambiguity on pass 3.

Complete this task with a summary naming the objective and the bar.

tasks.title: Produce the next revision
tasks.instructions:
The objective and the exit bar are in the "Inputs from upstream" section of this prompt, as the brief's structured output.

On pass 2 and later, this prompt also carries a "Loop History" section with what earlier passes produced and how each was decided, and your incoming input is the previous pass's judge verdict. Read the blocking items FIRST and address each one; if an item is not actionable, say so explicitly and explain why rather than silently skipping it. Do not re-try an approach an earlier pass already had rejected — the history is there so the budget buys new information.

Do the work itself, not a plan for the work: the judge inspects what you built.

Complete this task with a summary of what this revision changed, and make the captured `handoff` useful to a pass that cannot see this conversation.

tasks.title: Decide the verdict
tasks.instructions:
You are the loop's exit. Your captured `verdict` is what the engine reads to decide whether another pass runs, so it must reflect the work rather than the effort.

The exit bar is in the "Inputs from upstream" section, from the brief's structured output; the revision under review is the draft's output in the same section. INSPECT THE WORK — read the files, run what can be run. The draft's own summary is a claim, not evidence.

Decide against the bar and nothing else. Do not withhold approval because you would have done it differently, and do not approve work that misses the bar because the budget is running low — an exhausted loop is a recoverable halt an operator can decide about, and a false approval is not.

If you return `revise`, name every blocking item concretely enough that the next draft can act on it without guessing: what is wrong, where, and what would satisfy you. If you return `approved`, leave `blocking` empty.

Do not edit the work. Complete this task with a summary naming the verdict and its reasons.

tasks.title: Publish the approved result
tasks.instructions:
The approving pass's verdict is in the "Inputs from upstream" section of this prompt — the loop's outgoing edge resolves to the pass that actually concluded it, so what you see is the final revision's judgment and not an earlier one.

Record what was delivered in the objective's terms. The approval is settled; do not reopen it or re-review the work.

Complete this task with a summary of the delivered outcome.
